catalog_quote: The Chinantec languages are famous for their complex tone and stress systems. ... It is the stress (and its interactions with tone), however, that Chinantec is best known for. Syllables in most dialects of Chinantec can be stressless, can have a normal stress (called “controlled” in the literature), or can have what is known as “ballistic” stress. Controlled stress occurs on the final syllable of the word (although words are normally monosyllabic, so in practice this means stress occurs on the only syllable of the word), and is realized as vowel length and/or increased amplitude. ... At first glance, Ojitlán Chinantec appears to have a ballistic/controlled distinction (and in fact that was the analysis given in the original version of this paper). sweep_summary: One bibliography item only: Holsinger 1998 'Tone and Ballistic Stress in Ojitlán Chinantec', an unpublished University of Wisconsin-Madison ms. (Glottolog 303653) presented at the Jan 1998 LSA/SSILA meeting. Its full text is not online anywhere I could check (Crossref, archive.org, WorldCat, DDG/Bing: no hits; UW catalog 404); the only open text is the meeting abstract in the LSA 1998 handbook, already held by the project from the 9/16 check and now extracted to ( written there). The abstract is about the phonetic nature of ballistic stress (a [spread glottis] phonation type over a three-level tone system), not about stress placement, so the catalog's fixed: final syllable (in practice only-syllable) coding from Macaulay 1999 p.77 stands unchanged. It refines the catalog's tone_note: Macaulay 1999 (pp.77-78, fn 4; held by the project) reports Holsinger's ms. as showing no consistent ballistic correlates and five level tones, whereas Holsinger's own abstract keeps ballistic stress (as phonation) and a three-level system; the ms. (cited by Macaulay at pp.3-4) evidently developed after the abstract. Acquiring the ms. is medium priority (dedicated instrumental study of OC tone/stress, but unpublished; realistic route is to ask Monica Macaulay or David Holsinger). No new deciding source; Macaulay 1999 remains the catalog's the deciding source.

new_statements.quote: Instrumental phonetic analysis reveals numerous characteristics of OC that contradict many prior assumptions about this dialect. Among other things, the discovery of a 'very high' tone allows for a complete reanalysis of the tone and stress systems of OC. In light of this new data, OC can be described as having a more typical three-level system which then is affected by ballistic stress. Recent work by Silverman (1995), which suggests that 'ballistic stress' is better described as a phonation type than as a prosodic feature, is supported by the phonetic evidence at hand in OC. Acoustic cues such as postvocalic aspiration point to the association of ballistic stress with the feature [spread glottis], rather than features typically associated with prosody or stress.

new_statements.reading: First-hand instrumental statement on the nature of 'stress' in Ojitlán Chinantec: the ballistic/controlled distinction is a phonation-type ([spread glottis]) contrast overlaid on a three-level tone system, not a prosodic stress feature. It is silent on where word stress falls, so it cannot replace the catalog's positional rule (Macaulay 1999 p.77: controlled stress on the final, normally only, syllable of the word). It bears on the catalog's tone_note: Macaulay's summary of the same ms. ('no correlates of ballistic stress are consistently present'; five level tones) is stronger than what the abstract itself claims (OC 'affected by ballistic stress' as phonation; three-level system), so the tone_note should say that Macaulay's denial of a ballistic contrast is her reading of Holsinger's ms., while Holsinger's own abstract keeps ballistic stress as a phonation type.

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation is verbatim on printed p.77 (sec. 2.3) of the Macaulay 1999 PDF we hold (scanned), exactly as located. (2) Deciding source: a 1999 14-pp working-paper phonology sketch, the sole phonological description of Ojitlán Chinantec in Glottolog 5.1 (Glottolog lists 2 descriptive works; the other is a 1957/1962 proto-Chinantec mimeo). No reference grammar, dissertation, JIPA illustration or later acoustic study of this variety was found; SIL Mexico holds only the 1955 vocabulario, whose front matter (downloaded via the Internet Archive, read) gives four tone registers and no stress statement; the CIESAS repository's Chinantec theses are on Quiotepec and Temixtlán. Holsinger's 1998 LSA abstract (downloaded) concerns the ballistic-stress/phonation question, not stress position. So the best available source is held and quoted. (3) Caveat that keeps this at 'adequate' rather than 'well-sourced':

The Aclaraciones describe the orthography (j, h = glottal stop, r, central vowels, y), nasalization, and four tone registers marked 1-4 after each syllable ('El número 1 indica el tono más alto; el número 4 indica el tono más bajo'); no mention of acento/stress or ballistic syllables.

sources.note: Comparative treatment that (per Holsinger's abstract) analysed Ojitlán as four tone registers without ballistic stress, using the Smiths' data; would document the pan-Chinantec 'controlled stress = final syllable' generalization our quote relies on. Not Ojitlán-specific; unlikely to change the classification.
